There are several issues in this article. The jokes, the public's impression
and the defense strategy.

As far as the jokes go, I don't think they mean much. There are jokes about
lots of famous people. I don't know how many Bill Gates jokes there are. Jokes
are just something to provide a little interlude of laughter in the course of a
day. Truly mean spirited jokes don't raise laughter.

Concerning the public's attitude towards TK, the label of mentally ill, leaked
to the media, is much more damaging, simply because TK was right about the
public not being interested in reading a serious essay, if there were more
entertaining ways to spend one's time.

Those people who have read the manifesto know that TK has far more dimensions
than the media would have us believe these days.

Yet, public opionion doesn't necessarily mean much yet. It takes a while for
ideas to gain acceptance, and TK never said that this was an overnight process.
See paragraph 189, "Prior to that final struggle, the revolutionaries should
not expect to have a majority of people on their side..."

As far as TK's defense lawyers, I was crushed when he didn't get the defense he
wanted, but it's done now, and there's no taking back the past. I am only
hoping that on the day of sentencing, when he gets to make a statement, that
the childish sideshow about the president's personal life will not be taking
center stage.

TK has the chance in this statement, and in his furthur writings to change the
impressions of at least some of the public. Some people's minds can never be
changed, but then again, some people forget that they do have minds to make up
on their own.
